query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, the mechanically induced removal of an already thermally unstable passive film on the corrosion‐sensitive phase (e.g., the Al-Ni-rich/B2 phase) under elevated temperature accelerates local pitting and selective dissolution. This in turn leads to localized weakening that promotes further wear, so that the simultaneous action of elevated temperature, mechanical wear, and corrosive environment creates a positive feedback loop that amplifies both degradation mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: A lamellar eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a two-phase microstructure consisting of a corrosion-resistant soft FCC phase and a more corrosion-sensitive hard B2 (Al-Ni-rich) phase covered by a passive film that is marginally stable at elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to concurrent mechanical wear (sliding or abrasive stress) and a chloride-containing corrosive environment at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (room temperature and above, where the passive film is known to become unstable), in an acid/ chloride-containing solution; mechanical wear applied under controlled sliding conditions; and a baseline condition where wear and corrosion occur separately under matching temperatures and environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity (or lack thereof) of the thermally unstable passive film on the corrosion-sensitive phase which, when mechanically removed, exposes fresh reactive surfaces leading to localized corrosion and pit formation.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the passive oxide/hydroxide film (especially on the B2 phase) is unstable. When subjected to wear, this film is mechanically removed at specific locations, exposing the underlying phase to corrosion. The resulting pitting and selective dissolution further weaken the surface, which in turn exacerbates wear damage. The repetitive cycle of film removal and localized corrosion creates a synergistic degradation process that exceeds the simple sum of individual wear and corrosion effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched baseline (exposure to only wear or only corrosion), the total degradation under coupled conditions will be significantly higher. Both the wear rate (e.g., increased wear track depth and volume loss) and the corrosion rate (greater pit density and depth) will be elevated due to the interplay of mechanical film removal and rapid localized corrosion.
generation.baseline: The alloy subjected to isolated wear testing under a dry or inert environment and separate corrosion testing (without mechanical disturbance) at the same elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: The synergistic degradation is expected only when both conditions—an elevated temperature that destabilizes the passive film and an active mechanical wear process—are simultaneously present. Below the temperature threshold where the passive film becomes unstable or in the absence of wear, the effect should not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the synergistic increase in degradation remains uncertain and will depend on factors such as the exact temperature, wear load parameters, corrosive medium concentration, and microstructural heterogeneity distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical specimens of the eutectic high-entropy alloy and conduct three sets of tests: (1) pure corrosion exposure in a chloride-containing acid environment at the designated elevated temperature, (2) pure wear testing under identical temperature conditions in an inert or non-corrosive environment, and (3) simultaneous wear-corrosion testing. The tests should run for the same duration with carefully controlled mechanical load and environmental parameters.
measurements: Wear track depth and volume loss via profilometry
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM) to identify pit formation and film integrity
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to assess corrosion kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation (total weight loss, wear track characteristics, and pit density) observed under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions is not significantly higher than the arithmetic sum of the individual effects observed in the independent wear and corrosion tests, then the hypothesis that the coupling mechanism is driven by mechanical removal of an unstable passive film will be refuted.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperatures

Abstract: In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.

Conclusions: The effect of temperature on the passive and corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1
